Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. strengths: The paper addresses a relevant, under-resourced NLP problem and contributes a substantial document-level dataset: 2,508 ACL abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, including discontinuous, overlapping, and hierarchical structures.

EXCEEDS offers a conceptually simple unified formulation for trigger, argument, and sub-event extraction. The paper provides the loss, decoding algorithm, complexity discussion, hyperparameters, and computational costs.

The empirical study covers diverse global, discriminative, and generative baselines, three runs, five extraction metrics, ablations, complex-case breakdowns, and error analyses. Full precision and recall results are included.

The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices provide the schema, a complete annotated example, label distributions, annotation workflow, remuneration, and a concrete public data/code link. The limitations concerning abstract-only and NLP-only coverage are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central dataset contribution lacks adequate validation. There is no inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated sample, per-label reliability analysis, or human ceiling. A single primary annotation followed by inspection and a 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate do not quantify reproducibility, especially for subtle distinctions such as APP/MOD/FEA and WKS/MDS/PUR. Operational guidelines for selecting triggers, discontinuities, overlaps, and sub-events are also not fully specified.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not established by Table 2. The compared datasets use different ontologies, annotation scopes, tokenization, and representational capabilities; dashes often mean that a phenomenon was not annotated rather than absent. SciEvents is also not densest on several measures and covers only NLP abstracts. The evidence supports properties of this annotation scheme, not a general domain conclusion.

The grid representation appears non-injective. EAL records only an unlabeled trigger-head/argument-head link, while the argument role is stored independently on the mention-closing cell. If one span has different roles in different events, or overlapping mentions share a first token, Algorithm 1 can attach role-link cross-products to multiple triggers. No collision-frequency analysis, proof of lossless representation, or role-conditioned link ablation is provided, directly weakening the claimed support for dense overlapping events.

The baseline comparison may not use commensurate evaluation sets. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, whereas EXCEEDS handles the complete representation; it is unclear whether Table 3 removes unsupported gold instances for those systems. Baseline adaptations, complex-subset definitions, and subset sample counts are insufficiently documented to resolve this concern.

The reported advantages are small—0.51 AC and 0.53 EC F1 over the strongest baselines—with only three runs and no significance testing; the meaning of the ± values is not stated. The ablations do not isolate the grid formulation or document-level/long-distance modeling, and on rare cases they are unstable or sometimes outperform the full model. Reproduction also lacks the fixed split seed/IDs, token-to-subword procedure, complete refiner specification, exact early-validation schedule, and an analysis of the potentially exponential DFS decoder. These issues require important revisions before the work meets the soundness and reproducibility bar for Findings.

strengths: SciEvents addresses an under-resourced NLP problem with substantial scale: 2,508 abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments, including overlapping and discontinuous spans and hierarchical sub-events.

The dataset construction is unusually well documented. The schema was iteratively developed with domain experts, annotators received substantial training, every document underwent separate quality inspection, and the appendix provides schemas, distributions, an annotated example, tooling details, and remuneration information.

EXCEEDS is technically coherent and directly motivated by the target structures. Its multi-label token-pair grid unifies trigger, argument, and sub-event extraction and can represent structures unsupported by conventional span-boundary models.

The evaluation covers multiple discriminative, generative, and global baselines, uses predicted rather than gold triggers for EAE-only systems, reports three-run variance and precision/recall, and includes ablations, complex-case results, computational costs, and error analysis. EXCEEDS obtains the best reported F1 on TC, AI, AC, and EC.

The manuscript is clear and largely reproducible, with an explicit decoder, hyperparameters, complexity analysis, and stated public release of both data and code. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-3i5337fv/call-1aab655d5df44cd5a994a101c7221910/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality claim lacks quantitative reliability evidence. There is no inter-annotator agreement, double-annotated held-out audit, or measured post-adjudication accuracy. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a substitute, especially given subjective distinctions such as APP/MOD/FEA, MDS/WKS, and BaseComponent/TriedComponent.

Claims about intrinsic properties of the scientific domain are broader than the evidence. All documents are ACL abstracts, and cross-dataset density and complexity comparisons are heavily confounded by different schemas and annotation policies; the denominators and operational definitions for the reported complex-form percentages are also insufficiently specified.

The headline gains over the strongest baselines are small—roughly 0.30 to 0.71 F1—and no paired significance or bootstrap testing is reported. Moreover, discriminative systems are said to be evaluated only on contiguous-span instances, making it unclear whether Table 3 compares every model on exactly the same gold set.

Evidence for model generality is limited to the newly introduced dataset and a random in-domain split. An established benchmark, chronological split, or evaluation outside NLP abstracts would help distinguish a generally useful extraction method from one tailored to this schema.

The grid encoding has unexamined representational ambiguities: EAL links are untyped while argument roles are attached to spans, so a span used with different roles or overlapping nuggets sharing a head can induce incorrect cross-attachments during decoding. No oracle encode-decode reconstruction or collision analysis establishes that the representation is lossless on SciEvents.

The quadratic grid and potentially exponential DFS path enumeration are evaluated only on short abstracts, mostly below 350 tokens. Consequently, the document-level framing does not yet demonstrate practical scalability to full scientific papers. These limitations keep the otherwise sound contribution at Findings rather than main-conference level.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. The paper warrants main-conference publication based on its supported contribution and overall merits.

strengths: SciEvents is a potentially valuable resource: it contains 2,508 manually annotated ACL abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments, with explicit coverage of discontinuous and overlapping nuggets and hierarchical sub-events. This is relevant to NLP and materially larger than many compared domain-specific event datasets. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-a9o0ldyk/call-fab996797cc645a0be3d7e85f1ed52c0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The unified word-word formulation is well matched to non-contiguous spans and document-level event links. The paper clearly presents the representation, objective, decoding algorithm, ontology constraints, and quadratic complexity.

The empirical study includes diverse discriminative, generative, and global baselines; three runs; precision, recall, and F1; complex-case breakdowns; ablations; error analysis; and computational-cost reporting.

Reproducibility is supported by a concrete code/data release claim, detailed schemas and annotation procedures, hyperparameters, decoding pseudocode, and remuneration information. The paper is generally organized and readable.
weaknesses: The reliability and construct validity of the new dataset are not adequately demonstrated. Every document appears to receive one primary annotation followed by inspection, but no inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated audit set, post-adjudication error estimate, or quantitative schema-coverage analysis is reported. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a substitute for agreement, especially for distinctions such as APP/MOD/FEA and MDS/WKS that are evidently subtle.

The central claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not established by Table 2. Counts are confounded by ontology granularity and annotation policy; PHEE and Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several density measures, while dashes for complex structures in other corpora often mean that the phenomenon was not annotated. These comparisons establish properties of the resources, not necessarily their underlying domains.

The grid representation is not shown to be lossless. Argument roles are encoded on argument THL cells, whereas EAL is an untyped trigger-head-to-argument-head link. If overlapping arguments share a head, or one span bears different roles for multiple linked triggers, Algorithm 1 can create a cross-product of roles, spans, and events. Given the reported 33.70% overlap rate, a formal analysis and gold-grid encode/decode oracle score are necessary.

The claimed empirical advantage is fragile. EXCEEDS is not best on TI, and its gains over Tagprime are only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC points, with no significance tests and no definition of what the reported ± values denote. Moreover, removing the grid refiner improves TI, discontinuous AC, reverse-order AC, and sub-event TC in Tables 3–4, contradicting the claim of consistent degradation and weakening the proposed mechanism for complex cases.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently clear. Discriminative systems are said to be evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, potentially giving different systems different evaluation populations; EAE-only systems use Tagprime triggers while EXCEEDS uses its own predictions; and raw-text outputs from generative systems are not given a reproducible mapping to offsets when strings repeat. Baseline tuning and adaptation are also described only at a high level.

Both contributions are evaluated only on one random split of the authors' own corpus of 2019–2022 ACL abstracts. There is no external-dataset experiment, chronological or author-disjoint split, or cross-disciplinary evaluation, so evidence does not support broader claims about scientific-domain extraction or the method's generality.

The architecture largely combines established components—RoBERTa, BiLSTM, conditional normalization, word-pair grids, and 2D convolution—and is not adequately distinguished from the closest word-word relation formulations. Definitions and sample counts for complex subsets, particularly “reverse-order,” are also missing, while the acknowledged potentially exponential decoder receives no worst-case mitigation at inference. These unresolved soundness concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although focused auditing and controlled re-evaluation could plausibly make the work suitable for a later cycle.

strengths: The work is highly relevant to NLP and contributes a substantial resource: 2,508 scientific abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments. The schema explicitly covers document-level events, overlapping/discontinuous nuggets, and sub-event relations. A public data/code link is supplied. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-wtb6obf6/call-473779c4307d41c1ad306174348ddab3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The word-word grid is a plausible match for the targeted structures and provides one end-to-end formulation for trigger detection, argument attachment, discontinuous spans, and event hierarchy.

The empirical study covers several discriminative, generative, and global baselines, reports three-run variation and full precision/recall results, and includes complex-case, ablation, error, and computational-cost analyses.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Its appendices provide schemas, a complete annotation example, decoding pseudocode, hyperparameters, distributional statistics, annotation procedures, and remuneration information.
weaknesses: Dataset reliability is not adequately established. Documents appear to receive one primary annotation followed by inspection, but no independently double-annotated sample, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication agreement, schema-coverage audit, or post-inspection error estimate is reported. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a reliability measure, which is especially concerning for this subjective and structurally complex schema.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more complex is confounded with annotation design. The compared datasets use different ontologies, span conventions, document units, and policies for sub-events and discontinuity; preprocessing and the denominators of the complexity percentages are insufficiently defined. Moreover, SciEvents covers only ACL abstracts, while medical datasets exceed it on several density measures.

The grid representation is potentially non-injective. Argument roles are encoded on argument-level THL edges, while EAL is a generic link between mention heads. If overlapping mentions share a head, or one span has different roles in different events, decoding can create spurious Cartesian-product attachments. The paper neither proves representational completeness nor measures such collisions. Cycle handling and worst-case path proliferation in DFS decoding are also underspecified.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous instances, raising the possibility that systems are scored against different gold subsets. The mapping of offset-free generative outputs to exact occurrences is also unspecified, particularly when a surface string repeats. Complex-subset sample sizes are not reported.

The claimed advantage is statistically weak: improvements over the strongest baseline are only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC F1, with just three runs, overlapping variability, and no paired significance test. Some ablations improve TI or reverse-order extraction, while absolute discontinuous and reverse-order performance remains very low. The evidence supports competitiveness more clearly than a robust architectural advantage.

Important reproducibility details remain absent despite the release link: canonical split identifiers and seeds, the meaning of the reported plus/minus values, precise model-selection and validation-skipping schedules, subword-to-word alignment, full relation inventory, exact grid-refiner blocks, and details of baseline adaptations. The cost comparison also mixes GPU types and per-epoch rather than total training time.

The method appears incremental relative to established word-word grid tagging approaches, but the closest formulations are not directly compared or sufficiently differentiated. Combined with the ACL-only scope and lack of external-domain or temporal-generalization evaluation, this limits the case for main-conference publication independently of the soundness concerns.

Its BiLSTM/conditional-normalization token-pair grid, 2D convolution, successive-token and tail-to-head labels, and DFS decoding closely resemble W2NER-style word-word relation classification, yet that work is not cited or isolated experimentally. Baseline comparability and evaluation are insufficiently specified: several systems receive shared Tagprime triggers, substantial generative-model adaptations are only summarized, discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous representations, and the construction and sample sizes of complex subsets are omitted. EC evaluates a trigger-to-trigger correlation rather than correctness of the complete nested event structure.

The edge-union representation is not shown to be uniquely decodable: intersecting paths can recombine during DFS into spurious nuggets, and worst-case decoding is exponential. An oracle gold-grid reconstruction rate and collision analysis are needed, especially given the claimed prevalence of overlapping structures. strengths: The work addresses an ACL-relevant problem and contributes a substantial resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, including document-level multi-event, discontinuous, overlapping, and sub-event annotations.

The resource is documented with a detailed schema, event templates, split statistics, distribution analyses, and a complete annotated example. The authors also describe annotator training, separated annotation and inspection, remuneration, and a correction loop.

EXCEEDS provides a coherent unified formulation for triggers, arguments, and sub-event links. The grid labels, loss, decoding algorithm, hyperparameters, computational complexity, and hardware costs are described.

The empirical evaluation covers varied discriminative, generative, and global baselines, uses predicted triggers for EAE-only systems, reports three-run results with precision, recall, and F1, and includes ablations, complex-form slices, and error analysis.
EXCEEDS obtains the best reported mean TC, AI, AC, and EC scores, and the paper is generally clear, well organized, and candid about its abstract-only and NLP-specific scope.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is annotation validity. Production examples appear to be annotated once and then inspected, with no independently double-annotated sample, inter-annotator agreement, blinded expert audit, or residual-error estimate. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate measures workflow, not reliability. This is insufficient evidence for a benchmark whose event and role distinctions are subtle and frequently confused.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not supported by comparisons across datasets constructed with different ontologies and annotation policies. A dash can mean that a phenomenon was not annotated rather than absent, and PHEE or Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several reported measures. A matched-schema cross-domain study or substantially narrower claim is needed.

The ontology itself lacks validation of coverage and usefulness, such as an expert coverage audit, human upper bound, or downstream study. Several categories, especially MDS, WKS, and PUR, overlap conceptually, while some example triggers resemble rhetorical or semantic-relation annotations rather than conventional events. Operational rules for trigger selection, optional arguments, hierarchy depth, and coreference are absent, and reverse-order nugget is never defined.

The central model gains are modest: relative to TagPrime, the reported improvements are only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC points. With only three runs and no paired tests or confidence intervals, these differences are not convincingly established. Evaluation only on the newly introduced dataset and the absence of a controlled same-encoder alternative also make it difficult to attribute gains specifically to grid modeling.

The complex-scenario evidence is under-specified: subset sample sizes and precision/recall construction are missing, many baselines receive dashes because they cannot represent discontinuous or reverse-order outputs, and absolute EXCEEDS performance is only 13.86 F1 on discontinuous and 7.27 on reverse-order arguments. Moreover, stripped ablations outperform the full system on several of these targeted slices, weakening the claimed benefit of its specialized components.

The document-level and long-distance motivation is not directly tested. There is no sentence-versus-document context ablation, analysis by trigger-argument distance or event density, or evaluation on full papers; the documents are short ACL abstracts averaging roughly 175 tokens. Thus the evidence does not establish an advantage for global scientific-document modeling.

Although public code and data are promised, the manuscript omits several reproducibility-critical details, including word-to-subword alignment, maximum length and truncation, exact CLN and grid-refiner operations, distance-embedding clipping, optimization and checkpoint selection, split identifiers and random seeds, and precise baseline adaptations. It also does not analyze ambiguous grid encodings or decoder cross-products when overlapping nuggets share heads or paths. These concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation without further validation and reporting.

SciEvents covers only ACL abstracts, and Table 2 shows PHEE or Maccrobat-EE exceeding it on several density measures. Cross-dataset values also conflate domain properties with incompatible schemas and annotation policies; dashes for unannotated structures cannot establish their absence in other domains.

The grid representation is not shown to be lossless. Unioning HTL edges from overlapping nuggets can create spurious DFS paths, while head-to-head EAL edges can conflate mentions sharing heads. No gold-grid encode/decode oracle or collision analysis establishes that all annotated structures are uniquely recoverable. The potentially exponential decoder is handled only by skipping early validation, without a bounded inference procedure.

Baseline comparability is unclear. Appendix C says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, but it does not establish a common overall gold denominator. EAE-only systems use TagPrime triggers whereas EXCEEDS uses its own, so argument results conflate trigger and argument modeling. Other adaptations, serialization choices, and extra nugget-type supervision are insufficiently specified.

The claimed empirical advantage is fragile: the improvements over TagPrime are only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC F1, based on three runs and without paired significance tests. Several complex-subset variances exceed the gains, and removing the grid refiner or contextual module sometimes improves TI, discontinuous, reverse-order, or sub-event results, contradicting claims of consistent benefit. Test-subset sample sizes are not reported.

The experiments do not isolate the asserted benefits of document context, density handling, or long-distance modeling: there is no sentence-versus-document ablation, performance by distance/density, or evaluation on an established external dataset. Moreover, the HTL/THL construction closely resembles prior word-word relation formulations such as W2NER, yet the closest precedent is neither discussed nor directly compared, leaving the methodological novelty unclear.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including exact convolutional blocks, MLP dimensions and activations, optimizer and regularization settings, subword-to-token mapping, maximum length/truncation, validation schedule, model-selection rule, and seeds. Edge-level TI/AI/AC/EC metrics also do not measure correctness of complete reconstructed event structures. These combined soundness issues require substantive new validation and controlled experiments before a Findings recommendation.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial, relevant resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, including overlapping and discontinuous mentions and sub-event relations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-itbmjn3o/call-59004b712b884cc99268a6e4b071f6c8/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The annotation workflow includes expert schema iteration, trained professional annotators, separate inspection, revision, and remuneration reporting. The detailed schema and annotated example are useful.

The grid formulation is technically coherent and directly accommodates several structures that conventional span models cannot represent. The paper also reports three-run results, precision and recall, computational costs, ablations, complex-case evaluation, and error analysis.
EXCEEDS obtains the best reported mean on TC, AI, AC, and EC, and the released data and code could support useful NLP research.
weaknesses: The decisive soundness concern is annotation reliability. Documents receive one primary annotation followed by inspection, but there is no independent double-annotation study, inter-annotator agreement, adjudicated audit, or estimate of final label accuracy. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate measures workflow, not correctness.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more complex is not established by comparing datasets with different ontologies, scopes, and annotation policies. SciEvents' inclusive rhetorical schema itself induces many events and arguments, while most complex-form statistics are unavailable for the comparison datasets. Moreover, ACL abstracts support conclusions about NLP scholarly writing, not science broadly.

The baseline comparison is not demonstrably controlled: discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, unsupported systems receive insufficiently specified adaptations, and EAE-only systems inherit TagPrime triggers. Scores computed over different representable instances do not justify an unqualified state-of-the-art claim.

The improvements are small and lack significance testing: only 0.30 F1 for AI, 0.51 for AC, and 0.53 for EC over the strongest baselines, with overlapping three-run variation; EXCEEDS is not best on TI. Rare complex cases have no test counts and highly unstable results, such as 7.27 +/- 5.14 reverse-order AC.

The experiments do not isolate whether the grid specifically addresses density, distance, or structural complexity: there is no density/distance-stratified analysis, external-dataset evaluation, or direct comparison with the closest established word-word grid formulations such as W2NER. The presented ablations cover auxiliary modules and sometimes outperform the full model on complex subsets.

The representation is not shown to be lossless. Because EAL is untyped while argument roles are attached to spans, one span bearing different roles for multiple linked triggers can decode into spurious role-trigger cross-products; merged HTL paths can likewise create unintended nuggets. The paper neither states dataset restrictions that prevent these cases nor analyzes them.

Reproducibility is helped by the release and appendices, but important manuscript-level details remain unclear, including split seeds, preprocessing and subword alignment, optimizer settings, baseline adaptations, the exact ablation definitions, and how many initial epochs skip validation. These central, but plausibly correctable, concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial and highly relevant NLP resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, covering document-level multi-event extraction.
The schema explicitly represents overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical event structures that are poorly supported by many existing event-extraction benchmarks.
EXCEEDS offers a coherent unified formulation: multi-label token-pair relations represent nuggets, argument links, and sub-events, with decoder pseudocode and computational-cost discussion provided.

The evaluation spans several model families, three runs, ablations, complex-case subsets, error analysis, and precision/recall results. EXCEEDS obtains the best reported mean TC, AI, AC, and EC scores. The claimed public release, detailed schema, annotated example, hyperparameters, and annotation protocol also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Most decisively, the reliability of the central dataset is not quantitatively established. Official instances appear to receive one annotation followed by inspection, but the paper reports no independent double-annotation study, inter-annotator agreement, expert audit of final labels, or agreement by event component. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a substitute, especially for subjective distinctions such as Approach/Module/Feature and WorkStatement/MethodStep.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not supported by the cross-dataset comparison: density and complexity are heavily determined by each dataset's ontology and annotation policy. Missing complexity values are treated as unavailable rather than measured, while PHEE or Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several reported statistics. A same-schema cross-domain control would be needed.

Baseline scores are not fully commensurate. EAE-only systems receive Tagprime triggers, discriminative systems are reportedly evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, global systems receive nugget-type supervision, and generative interfaces are modified. The paper should state exactly which gold instances and supervision each reported score uses and provide common-denominator evaluations.

The performance advantages are small—about 0.3–0.5 F1 over the strongest alternatives on AI, AC, and EC—and no significance testing is reported. The ablations are also weak or inconsistent: removing the grid refiner improves TI and several rare complex-case scores, contradicting the claim of consistent degradation and providing limited evidence that the proposed components specifically solve density or complexity.

The complex-scenario evaluation lacks subset sample sizes and precise filtering definitions, and most baselines cannot represent discontinuous or reverse-order nuggets. Reverse-order and discontinuous performance is extremely low and unstable, so the broad claim of effective complex-event extraction is premature. Comparisons with structurally capable grid or universal-IE models are needed.

Important reproducibility details remain underspecified, including split seeds or fixed split identifiers, model-selection criteria, the number of initial epochs without validation, tokenization/truncation, exact refinement-block architecture, and baseline-specific configurations. Moreover, the stated overall quadratic complexity omits the decoder, which the appendix acknowledges can enumerate exponentially many HTL paths.

Broader scientific-domain claims are limited by using only ACL abstracts and evaluating only an in-domain random split. The paper does not test cross-year, cross-venue, or cross-discipline transfer, nor demonstrate downstream utility; related positioning against scientific information-extraction and discourse-structure resources is also incomplete. These issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising resource.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant, under-resourced NLP problem and contributes a substantial dataset: 2,508 abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments.
SciEvents explicitly represents document-level multi-event structures, overlapping and discontinuous nuggets, and nested events—phenomena that many existing event-extraction benchmarks omit.

The annotation workflow includes expert schema iteration, annotator training, separation of annotation and inspection, revision feedback, and remuneration details. These are useful quality-control measures.

The evaluation covers several discriminative, generative, and joint baselines over three runs and reports full precision/recall/F1 results, complex-case breakdowns, error analysis, ablations, and computational costs. EXCEEDS is competitive and obtains the best reported AI, AC, and EC means.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful figures and unusually extensive appendices containing schema templates, decoding pseudocode, hyperparameters, label distributions, and a complete annotation example. Code and data are stated to be public.
weaknesses: The decisive dataset-quality evidence is missing. There is no inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated sample, expert adjudication score, or post-inspection audit. A 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate does not quantify final precision or recall, particularly for subtle distinctions such as WKS versus MDS and Subject versus Object.

The central claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex than other domains is not established. SciEvents covers only ACL abstracts, and the cross-dataset statistics are heavily determined by ontology and annotation policy. Most complexity entries for other datasets are unavailable, while some reported datasets exceed SciEvents on event density, nugget density, or overlap. Missing annotations cannot be treated as evidence that a phenomenon is absent.

The ontology largely captures scientific discourse and rhetorical structure rather than events in the conventional sense; triggers in the supplied example include expressions such as “component,” “through,” and “effective.” This may still be useful information extraction, but coverage, semantic validity, and downstream utility are not independently evaluated. “Reverse-order nugget” is also never operationally defined, and one argument role has no test instances.

The grid encoding appears potentially non-injective. EAL records only an untyped trigger-head/argument-head link, while the argument role is stored on the argument span. If a shared span has different roles for different linked triggers, the decoder can cross-attach roles whenever both satisfy the ontology. Unions of HTL paths can likewise create ambiguous paths. The paper provides no oracle encode-decode test proving lossless representation of its annotated complex structures.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nugget instances, but does not say whether incompatible gold instances are removed or counted as false negatives; removal would make headline scores incomparable. Baseline adaptations are insufficiently documented, and predicted-trigger EAE results do not isolate whether EXCEEDS' small AC advantage comes from argument modeling or its better trigger classification.

The claimed methodological advantage is weakly supported. The main AC and EC gains over TagPrime are only 0.51 and 0.53 F1 without significance testing. Several rare-complexity results have large variance, and removing components sometimes improves TI, discontinuous AC, or reverse-order AC. There is no matched-capacity, grid-free ablation, no oracle/gold-trigger analysis, and no evaluation on an external event benchmark.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including token-to-subword handling, maximum input length and truncation, random seeds, exact refinement-block architecture, number of skipped validation epochs, micro versus macro aggregation, and definitions and sample sizes for the complex subsets.

Overall, the resource has promise, but the missing reliability validation, unresolved representation issue, and ambiguous experimental comparison prevent a sound Findings recommendation. These concerns appear addressable through a reliability audit, losslessness analysis, clarified/rerun evaluation, and stronger controlled experiments in a subsequent cycle.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial, relevant resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, including overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical structures.

The unified token-pair grid formulation is coherent and directly addresses structures that ordinary span-based pipelines cannot represent. The paper supplies a decoding algorithm, exact-match metrics, hyperparameters, computational costs, three-run results, and a public repository link.
The baseline suite is reasonably broad. EXCEEDS obtains the best reported TC, AI, AC, and EC scores, and the complex-case and error analyses expose genuinely difficult benchmark phenomena.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, with detailed schema definitions, a complete annotation example, dataset distributions, annotation workflow, and appropriate acknowledgement of its abstract-only NLP-domain scope.
weaknesses: The central dataset lacks convincing reliability evidence. Documents appear to be single-annotated and then inspected, with no independent double-annotation study, span/type/role agreement, adjudicated audit, or residual-error estimate. This is particularly concerning for subjective distinctions such as MDS versus WKS, APP versus MOD versus FEA, and BaseComponent versus TriedComponent; the 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate does not substitute for agreement measurement.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not established by Table 2. Comparisons confound domain with ontology, annotation granularity, tokenization, and document selection; dashes often mean that a phenomenon was not annotated rather than absent. PHEE and Maccrobat-EE also exceed SciEvents on several density measures. The evidence supports properties of this schema over ACL abstracts, not scientific literature generally.

The grid representation appears non-injective. Argument roles are encoded on mentions through THL labels while EAL links are untyped, so a shared mention bearing different roles for multiple compatible triggers can produce cross-product attachments. Likewise, merged HTL graphs can admit spurious reconstructed paths. The paper neither proves representational faithfulness nor measures such collisions.

The decoder can enumerate exponentially many HTL paths, as the appendix itself acknowledges, yet the complexity analysis characterizes the overall method as dominated by quadratic terms and omits decoding. The practical safeguard of skipping validation for the 'first few epochs' is also underspecified.

The empirical advantage is fragile: the headline improvements are only 0.51 AC and 0.53 EC points, without significance testing and against run-level variation of similar magnitude. Moreover, removing the grid refiner improves discontinuous AC from 13.86 to 14.98 and reverse-order AC from 7.27 to 11.99, weakening the claim that the proposed components specifically solve complex structures. Evaluation on an established external dataset is absent.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. Span-based models are evaluated only on contiguous instances, while EXCEEDS and adapted generative models support additional forms, but the common denominator and treatment of predictions in Table 3 are unclear. The false-positive protocol for the filtered complex subsets is also unspecified.

Important implementation details remain absent, including the exact convolutional refinement block, MLP dimensions and activations, maximum input length or truncation, optimizer and checkpoint-selection details, seeds, and the precise validation-start rule. Overall, the resource is promising, but annotation validity, representational ambiguity, and evaluation comparability prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The annotation workflow includes trained annotators, separate quality inspectors, iterative feedback, a detailed ontology, a complete annotated example, remuneration information, and extensive dataset statistics.

EXCEEDS offers a coherent end-to-end formulation that can represent several structures unsupported by ordinary span-boundary models, while the decoder and major hyperparameters are documented and a public code/data repository is stated.

The empirical study covers numerous discriminative, generative, and joint-extraction baselines; reports three-run results, precision and recall, ablations, complex-case breakdowns, error analyses, and computational costs.

weaknesses: The central dataset-quality evidence is inadequate. Official documents do not appear to be independently double-annotated, and no inter-annotator agreement, span/type-specific agreement, adjudicated reliability study, or independent expert audit is reported. A 73.05% first-pass inspection acceptance rate cannot establish consistency for this highly subjective and structurally complex ontology.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more structurally complex is not supported by the cross-dataset statistics: annotation scope, ontology granularity, and guidelines vary substantially across datasets, while discontinuity, reverse order, and sub-events are simply unannotated in most comparators. A controlled cross-domain annotation study is needed.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently specified. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous instances, leaving unclear whether Table 3 uses different gold subsets across systems. Mapping offset-free generations to exact document occurrences is also undocumented, and EAE-only systems inherit Tagprime triggers. These choices could materially affect the ranking.

The reported advantages are small—typically 0.3–0.7 F1 over the strongest baseline—and there are no paired significance tests or definition of the reported ± values. Moreover, removing components improves some discontinuous/reverse-order results, so the analyses do not convincingly attribute performance to the proposed modules.

The grid encoding is not demonstrably lossless. Untyped EAL edges combined with argument-role labels attached to spans can conflate cases where one span bears different roles for different triggers; shared HTL branches can likewise yield spurious DFS paths. This is especially consequential with 33.70% overlapping nuggets. No oracle encode/decode fidelity or collision-frequency analysis is provided, and the potentially exponential decoder lacks a test-time safeguard.

Important reproducibility details remain implicit, including subword-to-token aggregation, distance-embedding construction, convolution-block internals, loss aggregation, input truncation, split identifiers, seeds, and baseline tuning. The repository claim helps but does not replace a sufficiently precise manuscript description.

The method is closely patterned on established word-word grid architectures—pairwise grids, conditional layer normalization, 2-D convolution, and tail-to-head closure—yet the closest lineage is not adequately discussed or experimentally isolated. Together with evaluation only on a random in-domain split of ACL abstracts, this limits the case for broader main-conference novelty and impact.

Overall, the resource could become a solid Findings contribution, but annotation-reliability evidence, apples-to-apples evaluation, and validation of the grid representation are unresolved enough to prevent a clear Findings recommendation in its present form.

The document-level grid formulation provides a unified way to represent triggers, arguments, non-contiguous nuggets, and sub-event links; unlike several baselines, it can directly express all targeted structures.

The evaluation covers multiple discriminative, generative, and joint baselines, reports three-run variation, and includes ablations, complex-structure subsets, error analysis, computational costs, and full precision/recall results.

The paper is clearly organized and provides useful appendices containing the ontology, decoding algorithm, annotation workflow, hyperparameters, distributions, and a complete annotated example. It also reports public release of the dataset and implementation.
weaknesses: The dataset's reliability is not adequately established. Despite separate inspection and a reported first-pass acceptance rate, there is no independently double-annotated sample, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication analysis, or final error estimate. This is particularly consequential because distinctions such as MethodStep versus WorkStatement and BaseComponent versus TriedComponent are subjective and are also prominent model errors.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex than other domains is not supported by the cross-dataset statistics. The compared resources use different ontologies and annotation policies; several medical datasets are denser on individual measures, while dashes for discontinuity, reverse order, and sub-events often indicate absence of annotation rather than absence of the phenomenon. A same-schema cross-domain study or substantially narrower claim is needed.

The headline modeling improvements are small: only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC F1 over the strongest corresponding baselines. No paired significance tests or confidence intervals are supplied, and the modest ablation changes do not firmly establish that the proposed components cause the gains.

The comparison protocol is insufficiently clear and potentially not like-for-like. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous-span instances, whereas EXCEEDS targets the complete data; it does not specify precisely which gold annotations are retained for each main-table score. EAE-only systems also inherit Tagprime triggers, confounding argument modeling with detector choice. Common-subset and full-set results with explicit scoring rules are needed.

Important reproducibility details remain underspecified, including the exact relation-label inventory, treatment of the separately annotated nugget types, subword-to-word alignment, maximum input length, optimizer and random seeds, complete convolutional-block architecture, and the number of epochs for which validation is skipped. The DFS decoder also lacks a stated cycle or path-length safeguard despite allowing directed reverse-order edges.

The resource covers only ACL abstracts from 2019–2022, and there is no cross-domain, full-text, or distance-binned evaluation. Combined with an architecture composed largely of established encoder, word-pair grid, and convolutional components, this limits the broader case for main-conference publication. The promising resource is close to Findings quality, but the annotation-validity and comparison issues currently prevent a clear soundness recommendation.

strengths: SciEvents addresses a relevant and under-resourced NLP problem. Its 2,508 ACL abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments constitute a substantial document-level resource with overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical annotations.

The schema is documented with definitions and a complete annotated example. The professional annotation workflow includes annotator training, independent inspection, revision, and fair-remuneration information.

EXCEEDS offers a unified end-to-end formulation of trigger, argument, and sub-event extraction through token-pair relations, directly targeting structures that conventional span models cannot represent.

The evaluation covers numerous discriminative, generative, and global baselines, reports three-run variation and full precision/recall/F1 results, and includes ablations, complex-case evaluations, error analysis, and computational costs.
A public code/data URL, decoding pseudocode, major hyperparameters, dataset distributions, and candid scope limitations provide a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not established by the cross-dataset statistics. Annotation density is heavily determined by each dataset's ontology and guidelines; PHEE and Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several density measures, while dashes for complex forms generally mean that other schemes did not annotate them, not that their source texts lack them. Moreover, SciEvents covers only NLP abstracts.

Dataset reliability is insufficiently quantified. Despite the inspection process, the paper reports no inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated sample, adjudicated reliability study, schema-coverage analysis, or final error audit. This is consequential given the subjective distinctions among event types, roles, and nugget categories and the relatively low 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate.

The grid representation is not shown to be lossless. EAL records only trigger-head/argument-head links, while argument roles are attached separately to span-closing edges. Shared heads or a span serving different roles for multiple triggers can therefore lose the intended role-trigger pairing and induce cross-product attachments during decoding. Merged HTL paths can likewise create spurious nuggets. An oracle gold-grid encode/decode test and collision-frequency analysis are necessary.

Baseline comparability is unclear. Appendix C says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, without clearly stating how those filtered instances enter the overall scores. EAE-only systems use Tagprime triggers whereas EXCEEDS uses its own predictions, and the substantial baseline adaptations are not specified sufficiently. Common-subset, gold-trigger, and fully end-to-end comparisons are needed.

The claimed improvements are small: only 0.30, 0.51, and 0.53 percentage points over the strongest baseline for AI, AC, and EC, respectively, with only three runs and no significance tests. More troublingly, removing the grid refiner improves discontinuous and reverse-order results, and both ablations outperform the full model on reverse-order extraction, weakening the claim that the proposed components specifically solve complex structures.

Evaluation is confined to the newly introduced dataset, with no external dataset, cross-domain transfer, or controlled analysis across density levels. Complex-subset construction and sample counts are also insufficiently specified, especially for rare reverse-order cases with high variance.

Several reproducibility-critical details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including exact MLP/convolutional block definitions, token-to-subword alignment, optimizer and model-selection settings, split seed or fixed document IDs, and the number of initial epochs for which validation is skipped. The quadratic grid and DFS decoder also receive no peak-memory or practical scalability evaluation beyond short abstracts.

strengths: The paper addresses an important CL problem and contributes a sizeable resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts containing 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-iq7b4616/call-a8a4d9943ce54d33b107a87b994edaab/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SciEvents explicitly annotates discontinuous, overlapping, reverse-order, and hierarchical structures. The extensive schema definitions, worked document example, annotation workflow, quality-inspection process, and remuneration disclosure are useful.

The experimental section covers several discriminative, generative, and global baselines, reports three-run variation, precision and recall, computational costs, ablations, error analysis, and evaluations focused on complex structures.
EXCEEDS offers a unified end-to-end formulation and obtains the best reported mean TC, AI, AC, and EC scores, while being able to decode structures that several baselines cannot represent.
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality claim lacks adequate evidence. Despite a highly subjective schema with difficult distinctions such as WKS versus MDS and Subject versus Object, no inter-annotator agreement, independent double annotation, adjudication statistics, or held-out audit is reported. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate—based on a threshold of at most two inspector-identified conflicts—is not a reliability measure.

The claim that density and complexity are intrinsic characteristics of scientific text is not established. Counts across datasets reflect incompatible ontologies, annotation scopes, and guidelines; missing complex-form annotations in other datasets cannot be interpreted as their absence. Moreover, PHEE or Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several density measures. Applying the same schema to matched corpora from multiple domains would be needed for this comparison.

The grid encoding appears potentially non-injective. Argument-role labels are placed on span-closing THL cells, while EAL is an untyped link between trigger and argument heads. When one span participates in different events under different roles, or overlapping mentions share a head, the representation cannot necessarily associate each role with the correct trigger and may decode cross-product arguments. The paper provides neither a representational proof nor a gold encode-decode round-trip test, directly weakening its claim to handle complex events.

Baseline comparisons are not fully comparable. Appendix C states that discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous-span instances, implying different effective gold sets in the aggregate comparison. Baseline adaptations and tuning are also insufficiently specified, and no direct comparison is made with the closest prior token-pair/grid formulations.

The claimed improvements are small—0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC over the strongest baselines—and no significance tests are provided. Evidence for the proposed components is inconsistent: removing the grid refiner improves TI and several complex-case scores, including discontinuous and reverse-order extraction. Absolute performance on the central discontinuous and reverse-order cases remains only 13.86 and 7.27 F1.

The broad claims about document-level scientific event extraction are supported only on short NLP abstracts. There is no evaluation on another event dataset, another scientific discipline, full papers, or performance stratified by event density, sentence distance, or argument distance. The quadratic grid further raises untested scalability concerns for full scientific documents.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the repository link: the random split seed, optimizer, preprocessing and maximum-length policy, model-selection procedure, and complete refinement-block specification are absent. The random split also leaves the Reason role with no test instances, while only aggregate micro-style scores are reported. These soundness and evidence gaps prevent a Findings recommendation in the current form.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for ACL 2026, using the ACL Rolling Review overall-assessment criteria.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. Evaluate the contribution in light of its stated aims. Distinguish evidence of soundness from subjective interest, novelty, and prospective impact.

Findings requires adequate soundness and reproducibility. Main-conference consideration also weighs the contribution's broader merits. A sound Findings recommendation need not imply that the paper has a technical defect. Do not compute the overall assessment by averaging separate dimensions or treating personal excitement as a substitute for evidence. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Do not resubmit
The work requires fundamental reconstruction or lies outside the relevant research scope.

1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle
Substantial work is required, on a timescale longer than the next review cycle.

2 = Resubmit next cycle
Important revisions remain, but a revised submission could reasonably be ready for the next cycle.

2.5 = Borderline Findings
The case for Findings is close, with unresolved concerns preventing a clear positive recommendation.

3 = Findings
The paper supports a sound and reproducible contribution suitable for Findings.

3.5 = Borderline Conference
The main-conference recommendation is close; explain what limits confidence in that recommendation.

4 = Conference
The paper warrants main-conference publication based on its supported contribution and overall merits.

4.5 = Borderline Award
The paper is a plausible outstanding-paper candidate, with reservations about that distinction.

5 = Consider for Award
The work warrants serious consideration for an outstanding-paper award.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

strengths: The work addresses a relevant NLP problem and contributes a substantial resource: SciEvents contains 2,508 ACL abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments, including overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical structures. The manuscript and appendices were reviewed in full. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xuc4g6ce/call-32d38840809c4356bb6ad50ed8298f57/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The paper provides an explicit ontology, detailed label distributions, a complete annotated example, and useful information about annotator recruitment, training, inspection, and remuneration. The stated public release of the data and implementation is also valuable.

EXCEEDS offers a coherent end-to-end formulation of trigger, argument, and sub-event extraction using a multi-label token-pair grid. The equations, decoding algorithm, hyperparameters, complexity discussion, and runtime measurements make the basic approach reasonably clear.

The empirical study has good breadth: it includes global, discriminative, generative, and LLM-based baselines; three-run results; precision and recall tables; ablations; complex-structure slices; and error analysis.

The authors appropriately acknowledge that the resource covers only NLP abstracts rather than full articles or the broader scientific literature, and the modest absolute argument-extraction results leave useful room for subsequent work.
weaknesses: Annotation validity is not established adequately for a dataset paper. Documents appear to receive one primary annotation followed by inspection, but there is no independent double-annotation study, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication analysis, or post-inspection audit. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a reliability measure. Moreover, the appendix describes project logistics but provides few operational boundary rules for discontinuous, overlapping, reverse-order, and sub-event decisions. Given the subjectivity and density of this ontology, these omissions prevent confidence in the gold labels.

The central claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and structurally more complex is not supported by Table 2. Annotation density depends strongly on each dataset's ontology and guidelines, while SciEvents deliberately annotates broad rhetorical and propositional categories. Blank complexity entries for other datasets generally mean that a structure was not annotated, not that it is absent from the text. A controlled comparison using matched annotation guidelines is needed. The exclusive use of 2019–2022 ACL abstracts also does not support claims about the scientific domain broadly.

The construct itself needs stronger justification. Labels such as WorkStatement, Purpose, Finding, and triggers such as “through” or “effective” often resemble rhetorical or semantic-relation annotation rather than conventional event extraction. No human utility study, downstream evaluation, or comparison with scientific-information-extraction schemas demonstrates that the resulting structures capture the scientific knowledge users need.

The baseline protocol is not clearly comparable across systems. The appendix says discriminative models are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, whereas EXCEEDS is evaluated on the complete representation; EAE-only systems inherit TagPrime triggers; and adaptations of unsupported models are underspecified. The paper does not clearly define the complex-scenario filtering procedure or report its test-set sample sizes. Consequently, the state-of-the-art comparison may mix different prediction spaces and denominators.

The reported advantage is small: only 0.51 F1 over the best baseline on argument classification and 0.53 on event correlation, with three runs, overlapping variability, and no significance or paired testing. The grid encoding appears non-injective in important cases. EAL records only a link between nugget heads, while the argument role is encoded separately on the argument's THL edge. If the same span or head participates in multiple events or roles, decoding can cross-attach every ontology-compatible role to every linked trigger. Shared HTL paths can likewise create unintended DFS paths. The paper gives neither a losslessness proof nor an oracle encode-decode experiment quantifying such collisions, despite overlapping mentions being central to the contribution.

Evidence that the architecture specifically addresses document-level density, long-distance dependencies, or scientific-domain generalization is missing. There is no sentence-versus-document context ablation, performance-by-distance analysis, density-controlled analysis, external dataset evaluation, temporal split, or test outside ACL abstracts. Quadratic grid memory and potentially exponential DFS decoding are also evaluated only on short abstracts.

Reproducibility is improved by the claimed release and appendices, but the manuscript still omits exact split identifiers and seeds, baseline-specific preprocessing and tuning budgets, the precise epoch at which validation begins, and sufficient implementation detail for the grid refiner. Collectively, the unresolved annotation-validity, representational, and comparison issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although they appear addressable in a substantial revision.

strengths: The work addresses a relevant, under-resourced NLP problem and contributes a substantial resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts containing 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, including discontinuous, overlapping, and hierarchical structures. The dataset and implementation are reportedly public. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/acl2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-d_w0p0kf/call-45f50cdd4ba241b0b34588b60223d61f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The schema, annotation workflow, decoding algorithm, hyperparameters, split distributions, precision/recall results, computational costs, and annotator remuneration are documented unusually thoroughly.
EXCEEDS offers a coherent end-to-end formulation that can predict triggers, arguments, discontinuous nuggets, and sub-event links within one document-level token-pair grid.

The evaluation covers diverse discriminative, generative, and global baselines, reports three-run variation, and includes ablations, complex-structure subsets, and error analysis. EXCEEDS obtains the best reported AI, AC, and EC scores.
weaknesses: The reliability of the central dataset contribution is not adequately established. There is no inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated evaluation set, post-adjudication error estimate, or expert validation of schema coverage and downstream utility. A single annotation followed by inspection and a 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate do not quantify correctness, especially for visibly subjective distinctions such as WKS versus MDS and Subject versus Object.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more structurally complex is confounded with annotation design. The compared datasets use different ontologies, tokenization, span conventions, and annotation scopes; dashes for discontinuity or sub-events generally mean that a phenomenon was not annotated, not that it was absent. Moreover, Maccrobat-EE, PHEE, and GENIA equal or exceed SciEvents on several reported density or overlap measures. Evidence from ACL abstracts alone also does not support claims about the scientific domain broadly.

The grid representation is not shown to be lossless. EAL is an untyped link between nugget heads while argument roles are stored separately in THL labels. Arguments with multiple roles, overlapping nuggets sharing a head, or multiple events sharing a trigger can therefore induce spurious Cartesian-product attachments or merged event frames. Unioned HTL paths can likewise create unintended decoded nuggets. The paper needs explicit structural assumptions and an oracle encode-decode reconstruction rate or collision analysis.

The claimed quadratic complexity excludes the DFS decoder, which the paper itself acknowledges can enumerate exponentially many HTL chains. This matters both to the theoretical claim and to scalability beyond the short abstracts used here.

The state-of-the-art evidence is fragile: the AI/AC/EC gains over the strongest baselines are only 0.30/0.51/0.53 F1, based on three runs without significance testing. Complex-subset sample sizes are absent. Appendix C also says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous-span instances, leaving it unclear whether Table 3 compares systems against identical gold sets. Baseline adaptations are insufficiently specified, and no gold-trigger EAE experiment separates argument modeling from trigger-quality effects.

The HTL/THL formulation, BiLSTM plus conditional normalization, and two-dimensional convolutional grid closely resemble W2NER-style word-pair modeling, yet the closest predecessor is neither cited nor directly compared. The two coarse ablations do not isolate the proposed relation design; several complex-case scores actually improve when the grid refiner is removed.

Reproducibility remains partly dependent on the external release because the manuscript omits exact split identifiers and seeds, preprocessing and subword alignment, maximum-length handling, complete MLP/refinement-block definitions, the number of initially skipped validation epochs, and per-baseline adaptation and tuning details. These unresolved validity and comparison issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: SciEvents is a potentially valuable resource: it contains 2,508 ACL abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments, with explicit annotations for overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical structures. The paper states that the dataset and code are public.
The schema, annotation workflow, remuneration information, corpus statistics, and complete annotated example provide substantially more documentation than is typical for a new benchmark.

EXCEEDS gives a coherent unified formulation of trigger, argument, and sub-event extraction. The paper includes the loss, decoding algorithm, hyperparameters, resource costs, and an analysis of quadratic grid memory.

The evaluation covers several discriminative, generative, and joint baselines over three runs and reports precision, recall, F1, complex-case results, ablations, and error analyses. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The central dataset lacks adequate reliability evidence. Official documents appear to receive one annotation followed by inspection, with no reported inter-annotator agreement, independently double-annotated sample, adjudicated test set, or expert audit. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not an accuracy measure. The appendix describes workflow but provides insufficient operational guidance for exhaustive event identification, trigger and span boundaries, overlap, discontinuity, and sub-event decisions. This is especially concerning because several schema categories are semantically close, as the reported MDS/WKS confusions confirm.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more structurally complex is not established by Tables 1–2. Counts across datasets confound domain with ontology breadth, annotation granularity, tokenization, document selection, and annotation policy; dashes for complex forms generally mean that a dataset did not annotate the phenomenon, not that its texts lack it. PHEE and Maccrobat-EE also exceed SciEvents on several density measures. Moreover, only ACL abstracts are sampled, making the broader “scientific domain” framing too strong.

Baseline comparability is unresolved. The appendix says span-based discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, but it does not state whether non-contiguous gold instances remain as false negatives or are removed from their evaluation denominator. The latter would make the headline table use different test targets across systems. Baseline adaptations, document truncation, model-selection procedures, and tuning budgets are also insufficiently specified.

The grid representation is not shown to be lossless. EAL is a single relation between nugget heads while argument-role labels reside on nuggets; when one span has different roles for different triggers, decoding can form unintended role/link combinations. Unioned HTL paths can similarly create spurious nugget paths. No oracle gold-grid round-trip or collision analysis establishes that all SciEvents annotations can be represented and recovered exactly. In addition, the claimed overall O(l²) complexity omits the decoder’s explicitly acknowledged worst-case exponential DFS enumeration.

Evidence for EXCEEDS’s superiority is weak. Its headline improvements are only 0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC F1, comparable to reported run variation, without significance tests; it is not best on TI. The underdefined ablations produce small changes, and removing the grid refiner actually improves several complex-case scores. There is no comparison to a direct word–word grid baseline such as the closely related W2NER formulation, making the novelty and source of improvement difficult to assess.

The experiments do not isolate the paper’s motivating claims: there is no sentence-versus-document context comparison, performance by trigger–argument distance or event density, evaluation on another dataset, or downstream validation of the schema. Together with missing architectural details for CLN and the convolutional refiner, these issues prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation without important additional work.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial and highly relevant resource: 2,508 abstracts contain 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, with explicit treatment of overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical event structures.

The ontology, annotation workflow, quality-inspection process, annotator remuneration, label distributions, and a complete annotated example are documented extensively. The dataset and implementation are also linked publicly.

EXCEEDS provides a coherent unified formulation based on token-pair relations, with an explicit decoder and analysis of computational complexity. It can represent structures that many conventional span-based baselines cannot.

The empirical section is broad: nine baselines, three runs, precision/recall/F1 breakdowns, ablations, complex-phenomenon results, error analysis, and computational-cost reporting. EXCEEDS is numerically best on TC, AI, AC, and EC.
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality evidence is inadequate for Findings. Despite the subjective and structurally complex ontology, no inter-annotator agreement, double-annotation study, adjudication statistics, or independent held-out audit is reported. A 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate under an inspector-correction workflow is not a reliability measure.

The claim that scientific text is intrinsically denser and more complex is not established by Table 2. The compared datasets use different ontologies, tokenization, source genres, and annotation policies; dashes do not establish absence of a phenomenon. Moreover, Maccrobat-EE has greater event density, PHEE has greater argument and nugget-token density, and PHEE and Genia2011 have higher overlap rates. The evidence supports that SciEvents annotates complex structures, not that science intrinsically contains more of them.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, whereas EXCEEDS handles the full representation, suggesting potentially different evaluation supports. Several baselines receive different auxiliary information or modified interfaces, and Table 4 has no meaningful discriminative comparison for discontinuous or reverse-order cases. Closely related token-pair/grid structured extraction approaches are not evaluated.

The claimed gains are small—0.30 AI, 0.51 AC, and 0.53 EC F1 over the strongest baselines—and no paired significance tests or confidence intervals are supplied. The ablations do not consistently support the complex-structure motivation: removing the grid refiner improves discontinuous AC from 13.86 to 14.98 and reverse-order AC from 7.27 to 11.99.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the public link. The paper omits fixed split identifiers or split seed, run seeds, optimizer details, maximum input length and truncation policy, and a precise specification of the convolutional refinement block and normalization. The unspecified “first few epochs” decoding policy is another consequential implementation choice.

All model evidence comes from the newly introduced benchmark of ACL abstracts. There is no validation on an established event-extraction dataset or another scientific discipline, so the method's broader utility and the manuscript's general scientific-domain framing remain unsupported.

strengths: SciEvents is a substantial, relevant resource: 2,508 ACL abstracts containing 24,381 events and 56,411 argument links, with annotations for overlapping, discontinuous, reverse-order, and hierarchical structures.
The unified token-pair formulation is coherent and supports trigger detection, argument extraction, and sub-event linking within one end-to-end decoder.

The empirical study is broad, covering recent discriminative, generative, and joint baselines over three runs, with precision/recall/F1 results, complex-structure slices, ablations, error analysis, and computational costs.

The paper is clearly organized and provides useful reproducibility material, including a public release link, schema definitions, split statistics, hyperparameters, decoding pseudocode, annotation procedures, and remuneration details.
weaknesses: Dataset reliability is not adequately established. No inter-annotator agreement, independent double-annotation result, adjudication agreement, or audited test-set quality estimate is reported. The 73.05% first-pass acceptance rate is not a measure of final consistency, which is especially concerning for this subjective, fine-grained ontology.

The claim that density and structural complexity are intrinsic distinguishing properties of scientific text is not supported by the cross-dataset comparison. The datasets use different schemas and annotation policies; dashes do not demonstrate absence of a phenomenon; and PHEE or Maccrobat-EE exceed SciEvents on several density measures. Moreover, the corpus covers only NLP abstracts from one conference.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The appendix says discriminative systems are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, while Table 3 presents a common overall comparison without establishing identical gold denominators. EAE-only systems use Tagprime triggers whereas EXCEEDS uses its own triggers, confounding claims of superior argument or correlation modeling. The offset recovery used for adapted generative systems is also unspecified.

The claimed gains are small—0.51 AC and 0.53 EC F1 over the strongest baselines—and no paired significance or confidence testing is provided for only three runs. Ablations are marginal and mixed; removing components sometimes improves performance on rare complex cases, so the evidence does not strongly validate the proposed components.

The paper does not demonstrate that its grid representation is lossless for the annotated structures. Shared HTL/THL paths and untyped EAL edges indexed only by nugget heads can potentially conflate overlapping mentions or event links and generate spurious DFS paths. An oracle gold-grid decoding score and collision analysis are needed. The admitted exponential decoding worst case is also omitted from the stated overall complexity.

Methodological novelty is under-positioned relative to established word-word grid tagging such as W2NER, whose next-word/tail-to-head encoding and BiLSTM/conditional-normalization/2D-convolution architecture are very close but are neither discussed nor directly compared. Missing preprocessing, token-to-subword alignment, split seeds, checkpoint selection, and exact refinement-block details further limit manuscript-level reproducibility. These unresolved soundness and comparability issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
